title: Qt Testing: How to Test Qt Quick Controls Apps on Windows with testRigor
summary: Learn how to automate Qt Quick Controls testing on Windows with testRigor. Set up tests in plain English for buttons, dropdowns, dialogs, and more.

Qt is a popular framework for building desktop applications. With Qt Quick Controls, the app draws its own buttons, checkboxes and dropdowns instead of using the ones Windows provides. That is great for a consistent look, but it has often made these apps hard for test tools to read: a button looks like a label, and a dropdown looks like a plain text box.


testRigor can test Qt Quick Controls apps on Windows using plain-English steps. In this article we set up a suite and then go through a demo app screen by screen, showing the steps that work for each control.

## What Should Qt Testing Cover?


A Qt app is usually a set of screens built from the same few controls, so covering each control type once tells you a lot. Start with the controls your users touch most:


- **Buttons** and tab buttons
- **Checkboxes** , **radio buttons** and **switches** , including their checked state
- **Dropdowns** (combo boxes)
- **Text fields**
- **Lists**
- **Menus** and toolbars
- **Dialogs** and busy indicators


The demo app we use has one tab for each group. You can write one test per tab or run all of them in a single test, whichever suits your suite.


## Qt Testing with testRigor: How to Perform End-to-End Tests


Run tests against a copy of the app that is safe to click through. Tests that save or delete data should use a test account or a test database.


**Step 1** : Log in to your testRigor account.


**Step 2** : Create a new test suite and configure it:


- Enter a **Test Suite Name** , for example “Qt app”.
- Set **Type of testing** to **Native Desktop** .
- Under **Where to run the tests** , choose **Use testRigor infrastructure to run tests on provided application** , and set **OS** to **Windows** .
- Set **Number of test cases to generate using AI** to 0 if you want to write the first test yourself.
- Under **Upload file** , choose your app. testRigor supports` .exe` and` .msi` files (built for x86 or x86_64) and` .zip` files. The app is placed on the test machine’s desktop. What happens after the upload depends on the file type, which Step 4 explains.


**Step 3** : Click **Upload and Create** to create the suite. Qt controls are recognized by default, so there is nothing to switch on.


**Step 4** : Create a reusable rule that opens the app. testRigor does not launch a Windows app for you in every case, and every test has to start with the app on screen, so put those steps in a rule once and call it from each test. You create rules under **Reusable Rules** in the suite menu.


What the rule has to do depends on what you uploaded:


- **A single` .exe`** is placed on the desktop and started once, when the test machine is prepared, not before each test. If a test closes the app, the next test has to start it again, so the rule still needs to launch it after closing any old window.
- **A` .zip`** is only unpacked on the desktop. The rule has to open the unpacked folder and start the app itself. The sample below assumes this case: a zip that unpacks to a folder named` qt_app` containing` qtcontrolstest.exe` .
- **An` .msi`** runs an installer. The rule then has to open the installed app, and how that looks depends on your installer, so check it on your own setup.


The demo uses two rules. The first,` cleanup previous test` , closes anything left over from the previous test. It closes two windows: the app, and the File Explorer folder the previous run opened it from. If the folder window stays open, closing the app can return focus to it, and the next run will not find` qt_app` on the desktop.


```text
if page contains "Qt Controls Test" then
click "Qt Controls Test"
press alt+f4
wait 3 seconds
end


if page contains "Search qt_app" then
click "Search qt_app"
press alt+f4
wait 3 seconds
end
```


The second,` Open qt-control app` , calls the first and then opens the unpacked folder, finds the executable and starts it. Each test begins with that one line.


```text
cleanup previous test


click "qt_app"
press enter


click "qml"
press end
click "qtcontrolstest"
press enter
```


The screenshot shows this rule in testRigor. In your own rule, add a wait and a check at the end for something that only exists once the app has really started, for example` wait 5 seconds up to 20 times until page contains "Current tab: Tab One"` , so a launch error does not look like a pass.


**Step 5** : Open the suite and, on the **Test Cases** page, click **Add Test Case** .


**Step 6** : Enter a **Description** and the steps under **Custom steps new line separated** , then click **Add and Run** . The first test is just the rule, which proves the app opens:


```text
Open qt-control app
```


### How testRigor Finds a Qt Control


Three things are separate in a Qt app, and it helps to keep them apart when you write steps:


- The **visible text** on screen, such as the label “Preferred choice” or “Entered text: My new value”.
- The control’s **accessible name** and **role** , which Qt exposes to the operating system. In the demo app, the text field on the Inputs tab has no visible label, but it has the accessible name “Nickname”, and its role tells testRigor it is an input.
- The control’s **value** , such as “My new value” typed into that field.


testRigor finds a control the way a person would, by the text on it or next to it, and it uses the accessible name and role to tell a field from a label that has the same text. That is why` click input "Nickname"` finds the field, and why` check page contains "My new value"` checks something different from the field’s value. The roles shown in this article, for example for list items and menu entries, are what the demo app exposes. Custom QML controls can expose different roles, so check what your own app reports. SeeMaking your Qt app easier to test if a control has no name.


## Setting Up a Safe Environment for Qt Testing


A few things make Windows desktop tests more stable:


- **Start every test from a clean desktop.** A window left open by the previous test can steal the next test’s clicks. Close it at the start of each test, as the rule in Step 4 does.
- **Use a build made for testing.** Point the suite at a test build with test data, not at production.
- **Expect name clashes with other windows.** File Explorer has its own File, Copy and Paste. Use relative locators such as` to the left of` or` above` when a plain` click` is ambiguous.


## Test Case: Exercise the Controls of a Qt App


The demo app has six tabs. You can put the steps for all of them in one test, or give each tab its own test. Either way, a test opens the app with the rule from Step 4:


```text
Open qt-control app
```


To move to another tab, click its name, for example` click "Inputs"` . The steps for each tab below assume that tab is already open, so add the tab click before them. In one combined test, add it between the blocks. In separate tests, add it after the rule. The steps use the demo app’s control names, so replace them with the names in your app.


### Tab One: Buttons, Checkboxes and Radio Buttons


For this screen, the following tests are possible.


**Button.** In the demo app, a button’s accessible name matches its visible text, so a plain` click` finds it. If a button looks right on screen but your locator misses it, check the accessible name. When the same word appears more than once, say that you mean a button.


```text
check page contains "Button was clicked 0 times"


click "Push Button"
check page contains "Button was clicked 1 times"
```


To make clear that you mean the button, write` click button "Push Button"` .


**Checkbox.** State checks read the real checked state of the control, so` is checked` and` is not checked` match what you see on screen.


```text
enter "1" into checkbox "Check Box"
check that checkbox "Check Box" is checked


enter "0" into checkbox "Check Box"
check that checkbox "Check Box" is not checked
```


**Radio buttons.** Selecting one clears the others in its group.


```text
check that radiobutton "Radio One" is checked
check that radiobutton "Radio Two" is not checked


click "Radio Two"
check that radiobutton "Radio One" is not checked
check that radiobutton "Radio Two" is checked


click radiobutton "Radio One"
check that radiobutton "Radio One" is checked
```


### Inputs Tab: Dropdown, Text Field and Switch


For this screen, the following tests are possible.


**Dropdown.**` select` opens the dropdown and clicks the option, so it works with Qt’s popup list. You can also open the box yourself and click the item.


```text
select "Option A" from "Preferred choice"
check that page contains "Selected option: Option A"


click "Option A"
click "Option B" below "Option A"
check that page contains "Selected option: Option B"
```


If the option cannot be found in the popup, the step fails. It does not fall back to typing the text, because typing into a drawn Qt popup can select the wrong item.


**Text field.** To add to what is already in the field, click it first and move the caret to the end. The assertions read the label that mirrors the field’s value (“Entered text: …”), so they prove what the field holds, including the appended text. A bare` check page contains "typed 123"` could match any other text on the screen.


```text
enter "My new value" into "Nickname"
check that page contains "Entered text: My new value"


click input "Nickname"
press end
type " typed 123"
check that page contains "Entered text: My new value typed 123"
```


Use` click input "Nickname"` rather than` click "Nickname"` when the same text could also match a label.


**Switch.**


```text
click "Switch"
check that page contains "Switch is: on"
```


### Lists Tab


For this screen, the following tests are possible. In the demo app, list items can be clicked by their text, or addressed as buttons when the text also appears elsewhere.


```text
check page contains "No list item selected"


click "List Item 2"
check page contains "Selected list item: List Item 2"


click button "List Item 4"
check page contains "Selected list item: List Item 4"
```


### Menus Tab: Menu Bar and Toolbar


For this screen, the following tests are possible. In the demo app, menu bar entries such as File and Edit are not exposed as buttons, so click them by their text. Use a position relative to a neighbor when the same word also appears in another window, for example File Explorer’s own File menu or Copy button. Entries inside a menu popup and toolbar buttons can be clicked as buttons.


```text
check page contains "No menu/toolbar action yet"


click "File" to the left of "Edit"
click "Open"
check page contains "Last action: Open"


click "File" to the left of "Edit"
click button "Save"
check page contains "Last action: Save"


click "Edit" to the right of "File"
click "Copy" above "Paste"
check page contains "Last action: Copy"


click button "Cut"
check page contains "Last action: Cut (toolbar)"


click "Copy" to the right of "Cut"
check page contains "Last action: Copy (toolbar)"
```


The last two actions use different locators because of the names. “Cut” appears only once on the screen, so` click button "Cut"` is enough. The Edit menu entry and the toolbar button share the name “Copy”, so each step names the control by its neighbor.` above "Paste"` identifies the Edit menu’s Copy, and` to the right of "Cut"` identifies the toolbar’s Copy.


### Indicators Tab: Busy Indicator


For this screen, the following tests are possible. A spinner has no value to read, but it can have an accessible name that exists only while it is visible. The demo has buttons that start and stop it, so it stays visible long enough to observe. The spin box has a value, but testRigor cannot read it directly (seeCurrent limits ), so the demo shows it in a label that you can check.


```text
check page contains "Spin box value: 10"
check page does not contain "Loading spinner"


click "Start spinner"
check page contains "Loading spinner"


click "Stop spinner"
check page does not contain "Loading spinner"
```


In your own app, a spinner usually disappears when an operation finishes. Then test the result of that operation with a bounded wait, such as` wait 2 seconds up to 30 times until page contains "Import complete"` , instead of trying to catch a short “Loading” state.


### Dialog Tab


For this screen, the following tests are possible. The dialog’s text and buttons can be checked and clicked like anything else on the screen.


```text
check page contains "Dialog not yet closed"


click "Open Dialog"
check page contains "This is a dialog."


click "OK"
check page contains "Dialog result: OK"


click "Open Dialog"
check page contains "This is a dialog."


click "Cancel"
check page contains "Dialog result: Cancel"
```


## Making Your Qt App Easier to Test


A few choices in the app make steps shorter and more reliable:


- **Give controls a unique accessible name** (` Accessible.name` in QML). Steps find controls by name, so a control with no name, or a name that repeats on screen, is hard to target.
- **Avoid a visible label that repeats the text of the control it sits next to.** A step may click the label instead of the control.
- **Mirror typed text in a label.** Text typed into a text field is not exposed as the field’s name. Show it in a label and assert on that label.


## Current Limits


Qt can expose a value for sliders, spin boxes and dials, and progress bars are read-only. testRigor does not currently have steps to read or set the value of these controls, so in the demo setup their value cannot be asserted or changed directly. Assert on a label that mirrors the value, or use a button that changes it.


## Conclusion


Qt Quick Controls apps can be tested with the same plain-English steps as any other app: click a button, enter text, select from a dropdown, check a state. Create a Native Desktop suite, open the app with a reusable rule, name your controls well, and start with the paths your users take most, such as submitting a form, changing a setting and confirming a dialog.
